lesson.child_mission: A clause has a subject and a verb. Simple sentences use one clause; complex sentences join clauses to show relationships such as reason or time.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Mark the subject and verb in "The lantern flickered" and join it to "the wind rose" with a time or reason word.

FEEDBACK
Subject: The lantern; verb: flickered. Join: The lantern flickered when/as/because the wind rose — choose the meaning you want.

CHECK
A group of words without a verb is not a clause.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Identify subject and verb in eight sentences. Rewrite four as complex sentences using because, when or if. Explain how one join changes the relationship.

Write a short reflection describing one specific revision you made and why.

lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Identify subject and verb in eight sentences. Rewrite four as complex sentences using because, when or if. Explain how one join changes the relationship. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Original response on new material: Subject: The lantern; verb: flickered. Join: The lantern flickered when/as/because the wind rose — choose the meaning you want. Reasoning: I used clause by attending to subject and explain why it matters rather than copying the worked model.

Parent: Written model 2: Common error: A group of words without a verb is not a clause. Correction: Subject: The lantern; verb: flickered. Join: The lantern flickered when/as/because the wind rose — choose the meaning you want. Why: the correction restores accurate use of clause.

Parent: Likely misconception: A group of words without a verb is not a clause. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Produce a fresh example demonstrating clause on new material (not the worked model). Explain the particular words, sources or choices that make it work.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one likely error with clause, correct it, and explain why the correction helps a reader or audience.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
"Students waited" is one clause. "Students waited because the bus was late" joins a main clause to a reason clause.

TRY FIRST
Mark the subject and verb in "The lantern flickered" and join it to "the wind rose" with a time or reason word.

FEEDBACK
Subject: The lantern; verb: flickered. Join: The lantern flickered when/as/because the wind rose — choose the meaning you want.
teach_steps.explain:
A clause has a subject and a verb. Simple sentences use one clause; complex sentences join clauses to show relationships such as reason or time.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make decisions based on specific language evidence, rather than guess or copy someone else. Keep the meaning accurate and explain the choice.

HOW TO WORK
Read the original example and locate the words or actions that support the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Check your response against the feedback: did you address the same skill and show your reasoning? If a detail is uncertain, identify what would have to be checked. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than making the answer longer.
teach_steps.notice: A group of words without a verb is not a clause. Correct the meaning, not just the appearance.
